item.title: Trump’s Plan to Import More Ground Beef Is Falling Short
item.description:
Halfway through President Trump’s three-month gambit to import more ground beef to lower prices, little extra beef has been imported and prices have barely budged.

In August, Mr. Trump signed a proclamation allowing 300,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings to enter the United States at a reduced tariff rate. The additional beef could be imported over 90 days, with up to 100,000 metric tons entering each month in September, October and November.

But only 37,486 metric tons of this beef entered the country in September, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data, barely more than a third of the allowed amount. There hasn’t been much improvement in October, as just 21,937 metric tons entered through the 19th.

The lack of action is a potential blow to Republican candidates in the midterm elections. Mr. Trump said this month that beef prices “really became unacceptable to the voter,” and he has been trying to lower prices while keeping farmers and ranchers — typically a reliable Republican voting bloc — on his side.

Groups representing ranchers immediately criticized the president’s plan to import beef, saying it would lower what they received for their cattle; live cattle prices fell 3.4 percent the day the proclamation was signed. Ranchers said the threat that Mr. Trump would intervene in the market anytime prices rose made them more likely to send heifers and cows to slaughter instead of taking the risk of holding them back to help build up a larger herd.

“I am afraid they are trying to solve a short-term problem with beef prices, which will create long-term cattle supply problems in the process,” said Ford Drummond, the president of the Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association. Cattle prices have since rebounded.

And there is little evidence that any substantial discount has reached consumers, after Mr. Trump “encouraged” importers to sell beef at a 25 percent discount. The average price of a pound of ground beef fell 1.9 percent in September, to $6.79 from $6.92, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A year earlier, a pound cost $6.32.

Asked why most of the import quota was going unfilled, Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump is “delivering on his promise to consumers by reducing beef prices while allowing our American beef herd to grow.” She also said the president had “done more for American agriculture than anyone.”

The Agricultural Department and Customs and Border Protection did not respond to requests for comment.

The 37,486 metric tons of lean trimmings were imported in September under the customs agency’s “Affordable Beef” quota. But according to agricultural economists, it is unlikely that all, or even most, of that beef was imported solely because of the president’s proclamation. Some of it would have come into the country anyway.

The United States imported 1.9 million metric tons of all kinds of beef last year, with the bulk coming from Australia, Canada, Brazil, Mexico and New Zealand. Most of it was lean trimmings destined to be combined with high-fat trimmings from American cattle to make ground beef. An additional 300,000 metric tons would be significant, but pale in comparison with what already enters the country.

James Mitchell, a livestock economist at the University of Arkansas, used two different methods to calculate the amount of lean trimmings that would have come into the United States in September under usual circumstances, if there were no proclamation. One of the methods found that 41 percent of the 37,486 metric tons would have been imported, while the other method found that 79 percent would have been.

“Neither approach is perfect, but I think both are more reasonable than assuming all 37,486 metric tons were additional imports,” Mr. Mitchell wrote in an email.

From the beginning, it was unclear whether the president’s plan would meaningfully lower beef prices. Lean trimmings make up only a portion of the cost of ground beef; much of what the consumer pays for are costs like fattier trimmings, labor, processing, transportation and marketing.

Mr. Trump said he had a “commitment” that this beef would be sold at “25 percent below market prices,” though it is unclear if he meant retail or wholesale prices.

Ted Schroeder, a livestock economist at Kansas State University, said there would be no way for grocery stores to offer specific discounts to customers buying ground beef with these imported trimmings. It isn’t specially labeled, or labeled at all. Everyday meatpackers and processors receive meat from a number of different imported and domestic sources, and they don’t label them all for their customers.

“It is all stuff that gets blended, so there is going to be no way that I can think of that a product is labeled just that,” Mr. Schroeder said. “As soon as you start blending, identity preservation is just gone.”

Wholesale prices for domestic or imported lean trimmings, which vary by region, have barely changed, Mr. Schroeder said. And the small decrease in September’s retail ground beef prices is typical because grilling season is over.

“Is it a penny? Three cents? Four? Two and a third?” Mr. Schroeder asked, referring to how much cheaper the additional imports have made ground beef. “The reality is it is not going to be noticeable.”

item.title: A Simple Way to Benefit From Rising Rates: Buy Money Market Funds
item.description:
Rising interest rates have wreaked havoc this year in financial markets.

Yet they are an unambiguous boon in one unheralded arena: money market funds, where the higher rates almost immediately funnel more money to investors without major complications.

This is a big exception to the other major effects of rising rates, which have made plenty of negative headlines because they are a drag on the economy, a burden for people seeking mortgages and a punishing hurdle for stocks. In the bond market, rising rates are a complicated, head-spinning fact of life, setting off widespread losses, though they also promise better returns in the years ahead, as I noted last week.

In comparison, money market funds are blessedly simple. If you’re holding cash in them or are thinking of doing so, higher interest rates are something to celebrate right now.

That’s because money market funds closely follow short-term rate shifts by the Federal Reserve. On Sept. 16, the Federal Reserve raised its short-term policy rate, the Fed funds rate, one quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. Money market rates began moving higher almost immediately.

That said, they didn’t jump a quarter point overnight, as the Fed funds rate did. Money market funds are invested in short-term securities like Treasury bills, and it now takes about 36 days for all of these holdings to mature and be completely replaced with higher-yielding investments, according to Crane Data, an independent financial market research firm.

So while money market rates started moving upward soon after the last Fed rate increase, they have continued to edge gradually higher this week. The average interest rate for the 100 biggest money market funds tracked by Crane Data now stands at 3.71 percent. It was 3.51 percent at the end of August.

“If things go the way the markets expect, money market fund rates will reach 4 percent by the end of the year, and they will keep rising from there,” said Peter G. Crane, the firm’s president and a longtime expert on money market funds.

The markets assume that the Fed will raise short-term rates once more this year — but probably not at its meeting next week, which comes shortly before the midterm elections.

Inflation is likely to stay well above the Fed’s 2 percent target, according to estimates from futures traders, who expect the central bank to keep raising the Fed funds rate to a range of 4.50 to 4.75 percent by the middle of 2027.

If that turns out to be true, average money market rates can be expected to rise to somewhere close to 4.5 percent.

Rising short-term interest rates would probably count as more bad news for the economy, for multiple financial markets and for the great majority of consumers. But higher rates would only make the income stream from money market funds more appealing.

Globally, money market funds held $13.5 trillion at the end of March, according to the Investment Company Institute, the mutual fund trade group. They already have more than $8.4 trillion in assets in the United States alone, up from about $5.4 trillion five years earlier, Mr. Crane said. And as long as the economy keeps expanding and short-term rates remain above roughly 3 percent, the funds seem likely to keep growing.

U.S. money market funds aren’t insured by the government, as bank deposits are. If you prefer that greater degree of safety, by all means, keep your money in bank certificates of deposit or in high-yield savings accounts, where interest rates are rising, too. These various bank deposits are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.

As a consequence of previous financial crises, including a big one in 2007 to 2009, the rules governing money market funds have gotten stricter. Most money market funds for individual investors now hold government securities — mainly Treasury bills, which are backed by the U.S. government — instead of commercial securities, which are deemed to be riskier and are held by so-called prime funds.

I view big government money market funds run by large financial institutions as quite safe and keep most of my cash in them.

Money market funds are a form of mutual fund. As with stock and bond mutual funds, fees matter. Assuming the funds are invested in essentially the same underlying securities, lower fees mean higher returns, so check fund fees closely.

Vanguard, the low-cost leader in the mutual fund business, offers money market funds with fees ranging from 0.07 percent to 0.12 percent, a level that serves as a reasonable point of comparison, if you are shopping around. (Because my workplace retirement accounts are run by Vanguard, and Vanguard fees are low, the convenience of sticking with one place has led me to use Vanguard for money market funds, too. But your own situation may dictate other choices.)

We’re not talking about making great fortunes here. Money market funds don’t do that. They generate modest returns.

At the current average 3.71 percent rate for large money market funds, for every $10,000 held for one year, you would receive $371. That’s no bonanza. (Vanguard’s Federal Money Market Fund’s yield is a little better, 3.84 percent on Thursday, generating $384 for one year, at that rate.)

It’s better than the nearly nothing you would receive in a standard checking account. But in comparison with a hot stock, the returns from a money market fund are so small, they are barely visible.

Here’s a quick comparison of what you would have received, including reinvested dividends and interest, through Thursday for this year and over five years, for Nvidia, the S&P 500 stock index and the Vanguard Federal Money Market Fund. The data comes from FactSet:

Nvidia this year: 12.6 percent. Over five years: 56 percent, annualized.

S&P 500 this year: 14.1 percent. Over five years: 12.8 percent, annualized.

The Vanguard Federal Money Market fund this year: 3 percent. Over five years: 3.8 percent, annualized.

The money market fund looks a lot better when you stack it up against an investment-grade bond fund, however:

The iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond E.T.F. this year: a loss of 0.8 percent. Over five years: a loss of 0.1 percent, annualized.

The dismal bond returns occurred because rates soared this year, and bond prices and interest rates (or yields) move in opposite directions. The securities held by money market funds have such a short duration that the negative price effect of rising yields is barely discernible — and it is immediately outweighed by the income from higher yields.

Over longer periods, though, the situation is different. Longer-term bonds tend to outperform money market funds precisely because bonds carry higher yields as compensation for the risk of holding them for longer periods. That’s why it makes sense to hold bonds and bond funds for long-haul stability, and to use money market funds as a place to keep cash for paying the bills and emergencies.

The inferiority of money market funds as long-term investments is clear when you look at historical returns. Here are some comparisons with stocks and bonds, including interest and dividends, from 1928 to 2025, collected by Aswath Damodaran, a New York University finance professor, and posted on his website:

The S&P 500 stock index and its predecessors: 10 percent, annualized.

10-year Treasury notes: 4.8 percent.

Three-month Treasury bills, a rough proxy for money market returns: 3.4 percent.

There’s no getting around it. Money market funds won’t make you rich.

But in a time of rising interest rates, they are a convenient and immediately rewarding place to keep cash. When the news is bad, money market funds make me calmer. That’s no small thing in 2026.

item.title: Fearing Mass A.I. Layoffs, Some in Congress Eye Ways to Aid Workers
item.description:
The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has stoked fears that powerful computers might someday replace humans, leaving millions of Americans out of work and without a steady income.

It’s a doomsday scenario, one that could potentially overwhelm the government’s ability to care for the swelling ranks of the unemployed. And the mere risk has caught the attention of Congress, where lawmakers are starting to explore ways to bolster the nation’s economic safety net before it is too late.

In recent months, Democrats and Republicans have unfurled a series of bills that aim to offset the potential job losses posed by the advent of A.I. The ideas may differ in scope and cost, but together they reflect a widening trepidation in Washington that the government has fallen behind in preparing for vast technological change.

The latest proposal is set to arrive this week: a bill from Democrats including Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who leads his party on the chamber’s chief tax-writing committee, that would greatly expand the nation’s unemployment insurance program.

Existing jobless benefits cover a fraction of out-of-work Americans’ wages, generally for up to 26 weeks. Under Mr. Wyden’s bill, Congress would provide additional aid in times of high unemployment. Plus, there would be up to 26 weeks of further assistance to help those displaced by technology to learn new skills.

The bill includes other upgrades to a key federal safety-net program whose strains were obvious — and largely unresolved — amid the pandemic. With A.I., Mr. Wyden said, there is growing urgency to address those deficiencies, as the nation readies for “one of the biggest economic impacts on the economy in American history.”

“I think it would be malpractice to not get ready, because we’re in a position now where many citizens feel the looming fear of A.I. job losses,” he said. “And Congress has a responsibility to help the country get ready.”

The arrival of A.I. represents a seminal political test for the nation’s capital, where policymakers racked by division are slow to act except in times of crisis. The dynamic offers a contrast with the breakneck pace of development in Silicon Valley, where many believe that A.I. could auger swift and tectonic economic disruptions.

Speaking at a global conference this month, a co-founder of Anthropic projected that U.S. output could rise by almost 50 percent by 2030. But that same company’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, has coupled rosy growth forecasts with more dire warnings that A.I. could upend millions of workers’ lives.

For now, economists see no evidence that A.I. has altered the labor market on a grand scale. But there are still some emerging “A.I.-related hiring headwinds,” according to a report this week from Goldman Sachs, which found it has contributed to slower-than-expected job growth recently in some industries sensitive to technological change.

Martha Gimbel, the executive director of the Yale Budget Lab, emphasized that the signs do not yet suggest that A.I. is having a macroeconomic effect. But she also stressed that the work to measure those changes in real time was both “historically unusual” and difficult.

“In the middle of the Industrial Revolution, people weren’t trying to guess whether the weavers had been displaced yet,” she said.

The uncertainty has started to gain attention in Washington, where Democrats and Republicans have found common cause around the basic idea that the government should find better ways to measure the effects of A.I.

One of those bills, written by Senators Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, and Mark Warner, Democrat of Virginia, would require more robust reporting from companies about A.I.-related layoffs.

“I actually believe over a longer haul, five years plus, A.I. will probably create whole new categories of jobs,” Mr. Warner said. “But what does that do for the interim? And we don’t have good data yet.”

Despite bipartisan support, the bill and other, similar measures have stalled on Capitol Hill, where Republicans have largely followed President Trump in adopting a hands-off approach to artificial intelligence.

Bret Swanson, a technology expert at the conservative-leaning Heritage Foundation, said the reticence might stem from the fact that Republicans did not want to do anything to “disrupt these huge investments into A.I., which are sustaining what may otherwise be a rocky economy.”

That, Mr. Swanson continued, has affected even the debate over the implications for workers, which could “draw attention to the downsides” of A.I. in the eyes of a skeptical nation.

Mr. Trump’s top aides have dismissed any suggestion that A.I. could cause mass layoffs. In contrast, many Democrats still see wide-scale unemployment as a growing threat, and in response, party leaders have pursued measures meant to help Americans affected by technological change.

The roster of bills includes an attempt by Senator Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, to tax tech giants’ profits for a new federal trust. That would help fund benefits and training for displaced workers. Another, by lawmakers including Representative Greg Casar, Democrat of Texas, would tax tech companies and channel the proceeds to job-creating infrastructure investments.

But those efforts to boost the federal safety net face an even tougher political climb, given long-simmering disputes between the parties about the role of government and the provision of federal benefits. The result is a sort of stasis on Capitol Hill, despite a “high level of anxiety” on both sides of the aisle over job losses, according to Gina Raimondo, the leader of Raise Us, a nonprofit focused on A.I. policy.

“My great worry, actually, is that they’ll do what Congress often does, which is wait until it’s too late,” added Ms. Raimondo, whose group is backed by tech companies. She formerly served as commerce secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

There is also the thornier political question of who, exactly, should pay for it.

A handful of tech giants, including Anthropic and OpenAI, have publicly supported ideas that would set aside some of their expected new riches for Americans, especially those displaced by artificial intelligence. This week, Anthropic announced it would set aside a portion of its stock for a “public benefit fund,” and Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX, followed by promising to give away shares to “every kid in America.”

Otherwise, most tech companies have steered clear of endorsing specific bills in Congress targeting tech wealth. In the meantime, these companies and their executives have committed millions of dollars toward trying to elect tech-friendly lawmakers in the midterm elections, despite growing voter resentment.

Mr. Wyden said he believed that backlash was “starting to open some eyes” in Silicon Valley. But he acknowledged that A.I. companies had not endorsed his new legislation, called the Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act. The measure is backed by other Democrats, including Michael Bennet of Colorado, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Chuck Schumer of New York.

If adopted, the bill would raise the minimum level of unemployment benefits, which vary by state but on average cover less than half of workers’ past wages, according to program advocates. It would also expand the pool of people eligible to receive aid.

For the moment, his proposal does not have an official cost estimate, and Mr. Wyden did not include a provision to pay for the benefits, which currently are funded by employer payroll taxes. In other legislation, he has called for taxing tech giants and their data centers as a way to ensure that “big companies play a role” in offsetting their burden.

Still, Mr. Wyden added of the new legislative push: “There’s a lot of work to do.”

item.title: Canadian Cheese Was About to Become the Next Big Thing. Then Came the Tariffs.
item.description:
Cheese nerds are an excitable bunch. These days, if you want to see them get superexcited, just mention Canada.

Their eyes will light up as they tell you about the haul of gold, silver and bronze medals Canadian cheesemakers took home from the American Cheese Society awards in 2024 and 2025, including best-in-show honors two years in a row.

They may swoon over the organic operation at Fromagerie La Station in Compton, Quebec, where animal welfare is taken so seriously that the 150 milking cows rest on water beds after grazing in rolling Appalachian foothills 100 miles east of Montreal. They may chuckle as they talk about idiosyncratic characters like Jean Morin, the cheesemaker at Fromagerie du Presbytère, who converted a historic church into an aging cave where the wheels are turned by robots and who helped set a Guinness World Record for the largest serving of poutine. (It weighed more than three tons.)

Most exciting of all, they’ll tell you, is that these products and others are now for sale in the United States, many of them for the first time. “Some of these cheeses are as good as any in the world,” said Brad Dubé, who imports and distributes several through his Brooklyn-based firm, Food Matters Again.

Then, if you want to see how quickly excitement can change to a different emotion, ask about tariffs.

The 50 percent tariffs that President Trump slapped on Canadian cheese last month have caused havoc up and down the supply chain. Mongers and customers have had to cool their budding romance with Canadian cheese just as it was starting to get interesting. Makers who had been eyeing the new enthusiasm for their products from south of the border have put their plans on hold.

Some who were exporting already are not shipping anything right now. Like their American trading partners and retailers, they are hoping the tariffs are scaled back. While they wait, all of them are taking a hard look at how far they are willing to trim their margins.

“It’s immediately had an impact,” Mr. Dubé said. The momentum had been “quite real,” he said, but fizzled out on the news of the tariffs. “I have seen the downturn in my sales.”

The United States imports far less cheese from Canada than it does from Italy and France. Before crossing the border, Canadian cheese must pass through a thicket of quotas and regulatory paperwork. Until recently, most small-scale producers found the work too much to handle.

Simply sending a Canadian cheese to the American Cheese Society awards is an ordeal. Aspiring contestants have been turned back at the border. Since 2023, staff and volunteers at the University of Guelph in Ontario have smoothed the way by taking in every sample from about a dozen cheesemakers, checking the paperwork, retaining a customs broker, loading all the cheeses on pallets and sending them off in a refrigerated truck.

Mary Ann Ferrer, a professor of food science at the university, who leads the effort, said that when the cheeses arrive at the competition, “everybody there gets excited and even applauds.”

Fromagerie La Station entered the awards for the first time in 2024, the year it began exporting cheese to the United States.

“We thought, let’s just apply and see what happens,” said Catherine Durand, the head of sales and marketing. La Station’s cheeses won eight medals, including best-in-show honors for its Raclette de Compton au poivre, which has a spicy seam of pink peppercorns in the middle. “That was really, really amazing, and everybody was like, ‘Who are they?’”

Fewer people asked that question when La Station won best in show again the following year, this time with Alfred Le Fermier, an Alpine-style raw cow’s milk wheel.

Trade barriers help explain why the mere existence of great Canadian cheese comes as a surprise to many Americans. It’s also true, though, that artisanal cheesemaking in the country really took off only in the last 15 years or so, alongside an already thriving industry of larger producers turning out Cheddar and other cheeses. Once the craft movement coalesced, though, it moved rapidly.

“The Canadian artisan cheese scene has not been around as long as California’s or Vermont’s, but they’ve gotten to that same level of quality in a much shorter time,” said James Hanly, the sales director at Provisions International, a food importer and distributor based in White River Junction, Vt.

Craft cheesemakers had a head start because Canadian milk is of high quality, governed by strict safety regulations and an agricultural policy of price setting, production quotas and high tariffs on imports. Known as the supply management system, the policy was designed to provide basic economic stability for dairies, protecting them from the steep dives in milk prices often seen on open commodity markets. Supporters say that farmers who don’t lie awake worrying about foreclosure can invest in equipment, facilities and animal care.

“If farmers are able to make a reasonable living with what they’ve got, there’s less drive to cut every last cent of cost,” said Shep Ysselstein, the founder of Gunn’s Hill Artisan Cheese in Woodstock, Ontario. “That’s when things start to get compromised. You might not spend as much money on bedding, for example, which can impact the cows.”

One person who does not care for the supply management system is Mr. Trump. Calling it “discrimination” against U.S. commerce, he cited it as the rationale for his 50 percent tariffs in a proclamation in September.

After a short time of seeming to wait for the new levies to go away, as some of Mr. Trump’s earlier ones did, industry opposition has started to form. This week, a lawsuit challenging the tariffs was filed on behalf of Gellert Global Group, a food importer and distributor based in Elizabeth, N.J., which estimated that it could have to pay $40 million a year on the Canadian cheese it brings into the United States.

Thomas Gellert, the company’s chief executive, said in an interview last month that his firm imports Brie from Canada made with New York State milk, which is less expensive than Canadian milk. Tariffs on that cheese, he said, will hurt American dairy farmers and consumers.

A trade group representing cheese importers has asked for an exemption from the new tariffs for cheeses made with milk from the states as well as those made with Canadian goat and sheep milk. The United States does not have enough dairy goats to produce all the soft goat cheese Americans eat.

“The U.S. relies heavily on Canada and Europe for its supply of that soft goat cheese, and has for a long time,” said Mark Anderson, chief executive of Mariposa Dairy, a goat- and sheep-cheese maker based in Lindsay, Ontario. Goat milk is traded outside Canada’s supply management system, he said, so if that system is the reason for the tariffs, “it kind of misses the mark.”

For smaller cheesemakers that have only begun to test the American market, the tariffs may not put a huge dent in their finances. COWS Creamery, an ice cream and cheese company on Prince Edward Island, exports only a small amount of its distinctly creamy and grassy Avonlea Clothbound Cheddar to the United States, said Chad Heron, the chief executive.

“The most recent tariffs or bans or whatever nonsense Trump is up to won’t have a material impact on us, but it will cause a bunch of people a bunch of pain and that is too bad,” Mr. Heron wrote in an email.

Several other creameries had been planning to catch the wave of American interest in Canada. Whether they will move ahead or wait for the trade war to end is an open question.

“We actually already have a distributor ready to sell our cheeses in the U.S.,” said Bérangère Boivin-Côté, a manager at Fromagerie Médard in St.-Gédéon, Quebec. Médard’s soft, European-style washed rind cheese Le Cousin was the first runner-up for American Cheese Society’s best-in-show title in 2024, and everybody there believed momentum for Canadian cheese was growing in the states. “However, we know that entering a new market can be challenging especially with the tariffs that are currently in place.”

The math on a 50 percent tax is punishing for artisanal products. Even if everybody in the supply chain agrees to swallow some of the tax, most of it will be passed on to consumers, said Eric Frechette, an owner of Provisions International. And the new prices could stop shoppers in their tracks.

“On a cheese counter in New York, things that went for $40 a pound are going to be $60 a pound or more,” said Alex Brown, the wholesale cheesemonger for Gourmet Imports in Alhambra, Calif. “Which bumps them from higher value quality cheeses to precious luxury goods.”

For shops, unsold cheese very quickly becomes money wasted.

“We’ll be forced to either drop a product or accept astronomical prices,” said Marc Hernandez, the cheese buyer for Formaggio Kitchen, based in Cambridge, Mass. “That will be a risk, particularly when dealing with a perishable product that could go bad before we can sell it.”

A couple of years ago, when Canadian cheesemakers took home more than 20 medals from the American Cheese Society’s annual competition, I two questions: Why didn’t anybody tell me there’s great cheese in Canada? And when am I going to get some?

item.title: A.I. and New Rules for Accounting Are an Opportunity for Start-Ups
item.description:
For years in France, accountants have been more than just number crunchers, instead serving as important advisers to businesses of all sizes.

But artificial intelligence and a wave of new regulations are forcing the profession to adapt to an evolving world where balancing companies’ ledgers isn’t enough.

It is a change that software start-ups are seeking to capitalize on.

Among them is Pennylane, a six-year-old upstart whose bookkeeping software is now used by roughly a third of France’s small or medium-size businesses. Its success has driven its ambitions of expanding across Europe and has drawn the attention of big investors, who valued the company this year at about $4.25 billion.

“We think we can build a 500 billion-euro company,” Arthur Waller, a founder of Pennylane and its chief executive, said in an interview.

Pennylane aims to inject modern efficiency into a historically hidebound profession. Traditionally, businesses compiled financial information, sometimes gathered from scores of paper documents, and sent it to their bookkeepers through an array of unconnected software.

The result was often an out-of-date picture of a company’s finances.

And for years, the industry has been dominated by a handful of big companies, including Cegid and Sage, that sold bookkeeping as part of expansive and expensive software packages.

Pennylane offers what it likens to a financial operating system. Companies and their accountants work from the same platform — “a single source of truth,” according to Quentin de Metz, one of the company’s founders and its chief technology officer — to produce a quick and accurate readout of a business’s numbers.

The company, which is named for the Beatles song and began life with a small in-house accounting business, quickly switched focus to selling software to accountants. It pitches itself as an indispensable tool for accounting firms and ultimately for their clients.

Nearly all of the company’s business customers come through their accountants.

“People told us, Please don’t build something that will get rid of my accountant,” Mr. Waller said.

The company also adopted a charter with accountant-friendly policies, including a cap on price increases and a refusal to help customers switch accounting practices without their bookkeeper’s permission.

Pennylane’s tools have produced tangible benefits, said Laurent Lamoureux, the head of accounting services at BDO France, who first began using the start-up’s software four years ago. Bookkeepers can process clients’ ledgers much more quickly and cheaply, while customers can more easily get a handle on their day-to-day financial health.

Pennylane now has about 1,200 employees and hit 200 million euros, or $224 million, in annual recurring revenue. It has raised roughly $460 million from investors including Sequoia Capital, Capital G and Blackstone.

“When it comes to A.I. accounting, they are by far the most exciting company globally,” Luciana Lixandru, a partner at Sequoia, said in an interview.

National and European Union regulations may give companies like Pennylane another boost.

Last month, France began requiring many businesses to start receiving and issuing electronic invoices for tax purposes, using approved platforms to process the data. Thanks to its tight relationship with accountants, Pennylane says, it has about 20 percent of the e-invoicing market in France.

Pennylane is also moving into other countries, starting with Germany, where it has signed up nearly 1,000 businesses. Spain and potentially Britain are future targets as well, with Pennylane aiming to serve multinational businesses wherever they operate.

“We think we have an opportunity to create a European giant,” Mr. Waller said.

But rivals aren’t standing still.

Sage’s chief executive, Stephen Hare, told analysts last month that the software company was seeing “increasing traction” in e-invoicing. And Qonto, a fast-growing French banking start-up, has quickly emerged as a rival, buying up several accounting businesses.

Competition is increasingly making e-invoicing a loss leader that’s basically being given away, Mr. Lamoureux said.

For Mr. Waller and Mr. De Metz, the solution is to expand Pennylane’s higher-margin offerings, including banking services, inventory management and more.

The company is also adding A.I. features, including software that can automatically prefill tax returns and vibe-coding services so that customers can create their own tools on its platform.

The strategy speaks to a growing fear among accountants, according to Mr. Lamoureux: that they will be commoditized by technology. If practitioners don’t essentially become C.F.O.s of sorts for their clients, he said, “we are really dead in three years.”

Pennylane’s biggest opportunity, according to Mr. Waller, is persuading accountants that it can help with that.

“There will be automation,” he said. “You have a couple of years to demonstrate your value.”

item.title: A Tech Rotation Roils the Markets, Again
item.description:
Andrew here. Investors are becoming anxious after a week of pretty strong earnings. Why? There are jitters about the prospect that the U.S. will move aggressively against Iran after the midterm elections, and whether such an effort would end the war or complicate things further.

And will interest rates creep up even more? I’ll speak with Vice President JD Vance as well as Christine Lagarde, the European Central Bank president, about all this and more at the DealBook Summit on Nov. 18. Apply to attend here.

The stock sell-off looks set to continue on Friday, and investors are bracing for more pain ahead.

Surging oil prices and concerns about the cost of the artificial intelligence boom hit the Nasdaq Composite on Thursday, which had its worst one-day slide since June.

Analysts also linked the drop to reports that OpenAI may reduce the valuation target for its next fund-raising round.

The latest:

Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, traded near $115 a barrel on Friday. Oil looks set to post a third straight week of gains as fears grow of more fighting in the Middle East.

Nasdaq futures are under pressure again, adding to tech investors’ recent woes. Meta’s stock price fell nearly 7 percent on Thursday on concerns about its A.I. spending spree and its search for new ways to pay for it.

Watch the neoclouds, which sell computing power to A.I. companies. (More on that below.) Shares in companies like CoreWeave were sold off sharply on Thursday, and the yield on some of its debt soared, amid worries over the borrowing binge to finance A.I. bets.

Investors appear to be seeking out safe-haven assets. That has prompted a rally in U.S. government bonds. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note traded around 5 percent on Friday. That’s down from around 5.3 percent earlier this month but still well above the level on the eve of the U.S. war with Iran.

It’s a different story in Europe, where investors are on edge about France’s finances and the risk of more protests and riots this weekend.

Companies and the Fed would welcome lower borrowing costs. Traders have drastically dialed back the odds of an interest-rate increase. They now give a roughly 90 percent chance to the central bank’s keeping rates on hold next week.

Looking ahead: Pay attention to earning calls next week from Google, Microsoft and Amazon for any signs of A.I.-financing strain. Also look out for Anthropic, which is expected to file its public I.P.O. prospectus within the next few days.

In other market news: Shares in Verizon, T-Mobile US and AT&T fell in premarket trading on Friday on a Bloomberg article that cited unnamed sources to report that SpaceX was in talks with at least one major cellular infrastructure company to build a network of 80,000 cell sites. That could give SpaceX entry to the cellular service market.

A.I. agents have reportedly operated in bank accounts without permission. U.S. lenders have detected unauthorized artificial intelligence gaining access to customer accounts, sometimes taking actions that users didn’t agree to, Axios reports. Several lenders have started blocking third-party agents. The report adds to safety concerns about the increasingly popular tools.

Elon Musk is said to have invested about $1 billion in the Skydance media conglomerate. He is among the financial backers of the studio, Semafor reports, citing unnamed sources. Musk is a longtime friend of Larry Ellison, the tech mogul whose son, David Ellison, was the architect of the megadeal in which Paramount Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery.

The embattled law firm Weil Gotshal is said to be holding merger talks. Partners at Weil were told this week that it was in negotiations to combine with another American law firm, creating a top-10 practice by revenue, according to The Wall Street Journal, which citied unnamed sources. Weil has lost some prominent rainmakers in recent months, raising questions about its future.

California’s proposed billionaire tax could raise less than expected, some economists say. A new research paper by the economists Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh estimates that the levy would raise about $30 billion — far short of the $100 billion that proponents have calculated. The proposal, which is on the ballot next month, has drawn fierce opposition from several billionaires, some of whom have already left the state.

The subject of a big debate in recent days has been why Ukraine’s access to a military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service was throttled.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned that the move put lives at risk and suggested that he felt betrayed by Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX runs the network, and by President Trump.

Now The Wall Street Journal and The Times report that Trump called Musk to ask him to fully restore access to the satellite network, known as Starshield.

More from The Times:

Asked on Thursday whether he had made such a call to Mr. Musk, as first reported by The Wall Street Journal, Mr. Trump declined to say. “I don’t want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether ⁠somebody else called — doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line — he put it back,” the president ​told reporters.

When asked for comment, the White House pointed to Mr. Trump’s remarks.

It remained unclear on Thursday whether access to the Starshield network had been fully restored. Some Ukrainian officials said that was not yet the case.

DealBook asked on Wednesday what the consequences might be of letting Musk, a private citizen, wield enormous geopolitical power.

The cost of the artificial intelligence build-out may be rising, but demand for computing power remains high.

Among the companies seeking computing resources are providers of inference, or the process of actually running A.I. models and products. Data center demand for inference is expected to increase 36 percent per year through 2030.

The scarcity of what Silicon Valley calls compute is forcing inference companies to get creative in securing it, Sri Muppidi reports.

Some are squeezing more performance out of their resources. The inference company Together AI, for instance, is researching how to use Nvidia processors more efficiently.

“When you have a strong performance edge, it actually gives you more flexibility in terms of the cost of compute,” Dan Fu, a vice president at Together AI, told DealBook. “With our research, you can generate like two times, three times as many tokens per G.P.U.,” he said, referring to the processors most commonly used for A.I.

Other inference companies are striking lots of partnerships. Baseten works with 22 cloud companies. “Inference is a scale game,” Tuhin Srivastava, Baseten’s C.E.O., told DealBook.

He added, “As you get bigger, your ability to serve customers gets better from a cost perspective,” as does accommodating more of them.

And Modal Labs has formed a team to strike deals with cloud-computing providers, growing to 25 partners from four in just nine months, its C.E.O., Erik Bernhardsson, told DealBook.

Some are using alternative chips. Sail Research, which focuses on running A.I. agents over an extended period, is diversifying away from Nvidia G.P.U.s.

The company uses chips from Amazon, Google, Intel and A.M.D. That helps bring down costs for customers, Neil Movva, Sail’s C.E.O., told DealBook.

Others are helping build data centers. Together A.I. is working with Humain, a Saudi A.I. company, to erect a data center in Saudi Arabia that is expected to use 250 megawatts of electricity and feature 120,000 semiconductors.

Artificial intelligence is transforming a wide range of professional services. Accounting is among them.

But start-ups like Pennylane, a fast-growing French company, are betting that they can profit from helping bookkeepers through the transition — and navigating new rules that are changing the industry, Michael de la Merced reports.

The context: For decades, accountants in France (and elsewhere) have been more than just number crunchers, instead serving as trusted advisers to businesses of all sizes.

But the profession was hidebound in many ways: Companies often had to manually send financial information to their accountants, using software tools that were frequently unconnected.

Pennylane is part of a new generation of accounting software services. It is pitching what it likens to a financial operating system, in which companies and their accountants work from a single platform to produce speedy and accurate readouts of a business’s finances.

Pennylane rapidly seized market share by focusing on accountants. Nearly all its business customers have come through bookkeepers.

New accounting rules are hastening the adoption of these tools. Last month, France began requiring businesses to start receiving and issuing electronic invoices for tax purposes, using approved platforms to process the data. Pennylane now claims about 20 percent of the market for e-invoicing.

Other countries are set to adopt e-invoicing as well, a driver behind Pennylane’s effort to expand internationally. It now operates in Germany, with Spain and potentially Britain also prospects.

Luciana Lixandru, a partner at the venture firm Sequoia Capital, which has invested in Pennylane, told DealBook that expanding to the U.S. might also be possible.

“We think we can build a 500 billion-euro company,” Arthur Waller, a founder of Pennylane and its C.E.O., told DealBook.

The bigger picture: The advancing technology and e-invoicing requirements (and coming E.U. rules for digital processing of value-added taxes) mean that accountants have to provide more than just bookkeeping services to prove their worth.

If practitioners don’t essentially become C.F.O.s of sorts for their clients, “we are really dead in three years,” Laurent Lamoureux, the head of accounting services at BDO France, told DealBook.

Deals

In I.P.O. news: SB Energy, a data center developer owned by SoftBank, is said to be considering going public later than initially expected as the business of initial stock sales slows to a crawl before Anthropic’s potential market debut. (The Information, Bloomberg)

Infineum, a chemical company jointly owned by Shell and Exxon Mobil, has reportedly hired Bank of America to explore a sale of itself. (FT)

The financial communications giant FGS Global has hired Jeffrey McCracken, a former managing editor of CNBC, as a partner in its deals practice. (FGS)

Politics, policy and regulation

The artificial intelligence giants Anthropic, Nvidia and OpenAI each broke their own records for quarterly spending on lobbying in Washington. (The Verge)

“The Pentagon is quietly building an elite new tech sabotage agency” (Politico)

Best of the rest

Andreessen Horowitz, a longtime proponent of the cryptocurrency industry, dropped “crypto” from the name of a fund that invested in the sector. (Fortune)

Space junk is becoming a danger to people on Earth. (NYT)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.
